## Answer

**No.** The implication $F_{G_1}\cong F_{G_2}\Rightarrow G_1\cong G_2$ is **false**.

### Setup and interpretation

For a group $G$ with underlying set $S$, let $F_G$ denote the free group freely generated by $S$. A free group is determined up to isomorphism by the cardinality of a free generating set (its *rank*): two free groups are isomorphic iff they have the same rank. (This follows from the universal property, or concretely from the fact that the abelianization of $F_n$ is $\mathbb{Z}^n$, so $F_m\cong F_n\Rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^m\cong\mathbb{Z}^n\Rightarrow m=n$.)

Therefore
$$F_{G_1}\cong F_{G_2}\iff |S_1|=|S_2|\iff |G_1|=|G_2|.$$

So the question reduces to: does $|G_1|=|G_2|$ imply $G_1\cong G_2$? This is plainly false.

### Counterexample

Take
$$G_1=\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z},\qquad G_2=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}.$$

- Both have order $4$, so $|S_1|=|S_2|=4$, hence $F_{G_1}\cong F_4\cong F_{G_2}$.
- Yet $G_1\not\cong G_2$: $G_1$ is cyclic (generated by a single element of order $4$), while $G_2$ is not cyclic (every non-identity element has order $2$, so no element generates the whole group).

Thus $F_{G_1}\cong F_{G_2}$ holds while $G_1\cong G_2$ fails.

### Conclusion

The free group construction $G\mapsto F_G$ only "sees" the cardinality of the underlying set of $G$, discarding all of the group structure (the multiplication, identity, inverses). Consequently it cannot distinguish non-isomorphic groups of the same order. The implication does **not** hold in general.

### PROOF COMPLETE

For example, G1 = Z/4Z and G2 = Z/2Z × Z/2Z. Both have order 4, so F_{G1} ≅ F_{G2} (both are free groups of rank 4, i.e., F_4). But G1 ≇ G2 since one is cyclic and the other is not.

Therefore F_{G1} ≅ F_{G2} does not imply G1 ≅ G2.

Let me also justify that free groups are determined by rank. The free group on a set S has a universal property, and the rank (cardinality of a free generating set) is an invariant: free groups of different ranks are non-isomorphic (e.g., their abelianizations are free abelian groups of different rank, hence distinguishable). So F_{G1} ≅ F_{G2} iff |S1| = |S2| iff |G1| = |G2|.

The answer is No.
